newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says unemployment will turn this year - paper.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says unemployment will turn this year - paper.

text.p: Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he was certain unemployment figures would improve this year after they hit a new post-war record in January, a German newspaper reported on Thursday.
"I am sure that we can bring about a change in the trend this year," Kohl told Die Rheinpfalz daily in an interview excerpts of which were released ahead of publication on Friday.
A surge in German unemployment to a post-war record has piled the pressure on Kohl to produce results instead of optimistic long-term targets for cutting the jobless rate.

News on Thursday that unemployment had unexpectedly jumped more than half a million to 4.66 million in January dramatically widened the gap between Kohl's goal of halving the rate by the year 2000 and reality.
Kohl told the paper that the figures were the blackest during his 14-year term in office but he was sure they would get better because the economy was picking up slowly.
He expected proposed tax and pension reforms to help boost the economy. Labour reforms to make it more attractive to hire staff would help to create 100,000 to 200,000 new jobs.

"I still agree with Trade Union Federation leader (Dieter) Schulte and heads of industry that we must halve unemployment by the year 2000. I'm not saying we will reach this goal exactly, but the trend must go in this direction," he said.
Politicians from Kohl's centre-right coalition and the opposition quickly blamed each other for the debacle.

"The record unemployment clearly shows Kohl has failed and his misguided economic and financial policies have plunged the country into a dramatic employment crisis," said Oskar Lafontaine, chairman of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).

Protests rained down on Kohl after the Federal Labour Office in Nuremberg reported the unemployment rate had shot up to 12.2 percent in January from 10.8 percent in December. It was the highest rate recorded in Germany since January 1933.
"Germany with its 4.6 million unemployed is now stuck in the worst job market disaster since the Great Depression," said Ernst Schwanhold, economic policy spokesman for the SPD.
Kohl was urged either to speed up tax and welfare reform to boost investment and job creation, or find himself out of a job.

"We don't need any more fancy words and phrases," said Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary leader. "We need a real turnaround. We need lower labour costs and a genuine tax reform starting in January that gives companies real relief."

But Finance Minister Theo Waigel and other government leaders, while calling the latest data alarming, blamed the unemployment rise on the opposition for blocking his reforms in the upper house of parliament, which the SPD controls.

"The latest data urgently underline the fact that we have to act now," Waigel said. "The tax and social system reforms are now needed more urgently than ever before...Those who block these needed reforms are turning their backs on the jobless."
Waigel said he would press Labour Minister Norbert Bluem to accelerate the timetable for pension system reform.
Bluem said finger-pointing would not achieve anything. "Anyone who couldn't figure it out before should now know after these alarming figures that we all have to work together," he said.

Analysts said the unexpected jobless spurt would further strain already stretched budgets and raised the odds that Germany would fail to keep its deficit below the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product needed to qualify for the European economic and monetary union (EMU).
